ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Hartford, CT
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Hartford plant utilities, pressure equipment, bridges and steel structures. Request a site quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Testing in Hartford, Connecticut
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to Hartford and the Connecticut River valley around it for wall-thickness surveys, manual corrosion scanning and shear-wave weld examination on plant utilities, pressure equipment, tanks and structural steel. Work is performed at your facility under a written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III. To start, send the UT quote request for Hartford with the component, material, nominal wall and the code or customer specification that governs it.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Hartford

Hartford is known for insurance, but the metropolitan area is also one of the oldest manufacturing regions in the country. Engine and aircraft component work around East Hartford, Middletown and Windsor Locks supports a supply chain that Pratt and Whitney has described as largely small and medium businesses, with well over a billion dollars a year spent with Connecticut suppliers. Those plants run heat-treat and machining operations, test cells and process utilities. Around them sit hospitals and universities with their own steam plants, district energy and cogeneration systems, river crossings, rail corridors and the interstate highways that cut through the capital region.

Each of those facilities has steel that needs a reading. Steam headers and condensate return lines in utility plants thin where condensate collects. Compressed air, vacuum and coolant systems at machining and test facilities run through carbon steel pipe that corrodes from the inside where moisture is trapped. Hydraulic and quench tanks, pressure receivers and process vessels have inspection plans that call for periodic thickness data. Outside the fence, the Connecticut Department of Transportation is rehabilitating the I-84 viaduct bridges through downtown Hartford to address deterioration of their superstructure and substructure, and bridge steel brings its own ultrasonic questions about plate thickness and welded details.

Connecticut's old industrial buildings add another reason for survey work. Many plants occupy structures and utility systems that are many decades old, and when ownership or production changes, a baseline ultrasonic survey tells engineers where metal has been lost before a repair budget is set.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it does not

An ultrasonic instrument launches a short sound pulse through a coupled probe and times the echo from the far wall or from a reflector inside the metal. That timing becomes either a thickness reading or a position and amplitude for a flaw. Thickness work answers how much wall is left. Angle-beam shear-wave work answers whether a weld contains planar defects such as lack of fusion, cracks or slag that sit below the surface where magnetic particle and penetrant methods cannot see.

The method has boundaries a competent technician states plainly. Sound will not cross an air gap, so the probe must be coupled to a surface that is clean and reasonably smooth. Rough castings, cast stainless and austenitic welds scatter the beam and can hide small flaws. Thin wall, laminations and deep pitting produce confusing echoes, and a single digital reading from a gauge can be wrong if the probe straddles a pit. The countermeasures are dual-element probes designed for corroded surfaces, an A-scan display so the operator reads the waveform, and calibration on a step block made of the same material across the expected range. The national ultrasonic testing page covers the method in general; this one applies it to Hartford work.

Beam geometry limits coverage on welds as well. A flaw oriented parallel to the beam may reflect little energy, so welds are scanned from both sides where access allows, and the report states any area that could not be covered.

Codes and the Connecticut framework

The governing document decides the examination and the acceptance. ASME Section VIII Division 1 vessels use Mandatory Appendix 12 for ultrasonic weld examination and its acceptance standards. ASME B31.3 process piping uses paragraph 344.6 with criteria in Table 341.3.2, and B31.1 covers power piping typical of steam plants. Beneath these sits ASME Section V: Article 4 for weld examination, Article 5 for material examination and Article 23 for the contact thickness practice, with ASTM E797 as the companion standard for contact thickness measurement. Structural groove welds fall under AWS D1.1, while steel highway bridges follow AWS D1.5 under owner specification. For plain-language background, see our guide to ASME Section V Article 5.

Connecticut regulates boilers by statute. Chapter 540 of the General Statutes requires that boilers be inspected and operated under a certificate, and it provides for state boiler inspectors, insurance company inspectors who hold certificates of competency, and special inspectors who pass an examination. The Office of the State Building Inspector administers boiler inspections. How a particular pressure vessel is classified under that scheme is something to confirm with the jurisdiction and your insurer. Atlantis is not an inspector under that scheme; we perform ultrasonic examination, record the data and give it to the responsible inspector. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector likewise remains responsible for integrity decisions.

Many Hartford-area suppliers also work to customer requirements, including specifications flowed down by their own customers for in-house examination of tooling, utilities and weldments. If a customer standard governs a job, provide it with the quote request and we will confirm how the procedure and report address it. We do not claim that SNT-TC-1A qualification by itself satisfies any particular customer's requirement.

Technique for thickness surveys

A well-run survey begins with a plan of condition monitoring locations on a drawing or isometric, so that the same spots are read each cycle. On site, the technician prepares each point, applies couplant and calibrates on a step block of matching material. Readings on corroded carbon steel use dual-element probes, and the technician watches the A-scan for the echo pattern that distinguishes a true back wall from a lamination or a doubled signal. Where wall is thin, the technician checks the near-surface response before trusting any figure.

Hot piping needs correction. Sound velocity changes with temperature, and standard probes and couplants cannot tolerate very hot surfaces, so high-temperature probes and couplants are used on steam and thermal oil systems, and surface temperature is logged with the readings. Grid readings are used on tank shells and flat surfaces, and a thin area found during the survey is flagged immediately so your inspector can ask for a denser grid before the crew leaves.

Technique for ultrasonic weld examination

Weld work uses angle-beam shear-wave probes, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, selected for thickness and joint geometry. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes, and the technician scans the weld volume from the accessible faces. Indications are located, sized by length and compared with the reference. Evaluation follows the criteria of the named code. Because interpretation matters, Level II technicians perform this work and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure before it starts.

Surface condition controls what can be scanned. Weld crowns, spatter and heavy coating may need dressing. For bridge and heavy structural steel, access by lift or scaffold and traffic protection are planned with the owner or contractor before anyone starts scanning.

Using thickness data after the survey

Thickness readings become useful when they are trended. An engineer compares each location with its earlier reading to calculate a corrosion rate and an estimated remaining life, then decides whether to repair, monitor more closely or change the inspection interval. We keep location labels identical from one survey to the next, and we note any change in probe, instrument or surface condition so differences in the data are not mistaken for differences in the steel.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in Hartford. Technicians are mobilized to your facility for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, where certification is the employer's responsibility. A Level II sets up and calibrates the equipment and performs and interprets the examination; an ASNT Level III establishes techniques, approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for its management system, which covers how we control documents and records.

What the report contains

The report identifies the component and every reading location, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the technician and level, and surface temperature where it matters. Thickness work is presented as a table or a grid of readings against nominal and minimum wall. Weld work lists each recordable indication with its position, length, depth and amplitude relative to the reference, followed by a clear accept or reject against the stated criteria, with sketches that show location. Raw data can be supplied in a format that suits your inspection database.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Hartford

New England weather sets the calendar for exterior work. Freezing surfaces thicken couplant and stress batteries and displays, so outdoor piping, tanks and bridge members may need heated couplant, windbreaks or a milder day. Summer sun can raise exposed steel above the comfortable range for ordinary probes. Utility and manufacturing outages cluster around production schedules, so early notice avoids collisions with other trades.

Access and safety rules matter. Hospitals, universities and aerospace-related plants commonly require escorts, background checks, tool inventories and safety orientation before contractors enter. Interstate 84 and Interstate 91 meet in the city, and construction on the I-84 corridor can affect travel; we agree timing with your supervisor and do not promise an arrival window. Tell us whether lines are in service, whether the area is a confined space and whether hot work is nearby.

UT, MT or PT: choosing the method in Hartford

Choose UT for thickness and for internal weld flaws. If the question is a surface crack in carbon steel, see magnetic particle inspection in Hartford. For stainless, aluminum, titanium or nickel alloys, see liquid penetrant testing in Hartford. Repairs often combine UT before and PT or MT after the weld.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Hartford-area employers can build in-house capability through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with practice on the ultrasonic testing simulator. The NDT training page for East Hartford explains how courses are delivered to employers in the capital region, and our written practice development service helps you set the program under which you qualify your own staff.

faq.q: What does an ultrasonic thickness survey include in Hartford?
faq.a: We prepare marked locations, couple the probe, calibrate on a step block of matching material and record remaining wall at each condition monitoring location. Results are tabulated against nominal and minimum thickness so your inspector can trend corrosion.

faq.q: Can you ultrasonically examine welds on bridge steel or structural frames?
faq.a: Yes. Level II technicians examine groove welds with angle-beam probes and a reference curve, then evaluate indications against the criteria you name, such as AWS D1.1 for buildings or AWS D1.5 for bridges, under an approved written procedure.

faq.q: Who is responsible for boiler and pressure vessel inspection in Connecticut?
faq.a: Connecticut's boiler statute provides for state inspectors, insurance company inspectors and special inspectors. Atlantis is not one of them; we perform ultrasonic examination and give the data to the responsible inspector for their decisions.

faq.q: Can UT be used on stainless steel and cast components?
faq.a: Sometimes, but coarse grain and austenitic weld structure scatter sound and reduce reliability. We review the material first and may propose same-alloy reference blocks, a modified technique or another method when UT is a poor fit.

faq.q: How should surfaces be prepared before ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, flaking paint and spatter at the reading spots and dress high weld crowns where angle-beam scanning is planned. A clean, smooth, coupled surface prevents unreadable echoes and false thickness values.

faq.q: What should I include when requesting a UT quote for a Hartford site?
faq.a: Include component type, material, nominal thickness, governing code or customer specification, the number of locations or weld length, access conditions, service status and site safety rules. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Does your qualification satisfy our customer's aerospace requirements?
faq.a: Our technicians are qualified under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Whether that satisfies a specific customer flow-down depends on that customer's document, so send it with your request and we will confirm what can be provided.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography for a weld?
faq.a: Only if the construction code permits it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before work starts. Some codes include ultrasonic provisions for production welds, but acceptance rules differ from radiographic criteria.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians in ultrasonic thickness gauging?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses with an ASNT Level III instructor and simulator practice. Your company qualifies and certifies its own personnel under its written practice following SNT-TC-1A.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Hartford, CT | MT
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing of steel welds, bridge details, tooling and plant structures in Hartford, CT. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Hartford, Connecticut
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT travels to Hartford and the capital region to carry out magnetic particle inspection (MPI), sometimes called mag particle testing, on carbon and low-alloy steel welds, shafts, gear and tooling steel, lifting equipment and structural connections. A portable yoke and the right particles reveal surface and near-surface cracks that visual checks miss. Send the MT quote request for Hartford with the component, material, code or customer procedure, and the number of welds or parts.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Hartford

The Hartford area has been a center of precision metalworking since the nineteenth century, and it still is. East Hartford and Middletown host engine manufacturing, Windsor Locks has an aerospace systems plant, and a web of machine shops, forging users and fabricators around them supply the work. These businesses use huge amounts of ferromagnetic steel that never leaves the plant: presses and press frames, die and fixture steel, gearbox and drive components, overhead cranes, heat-treat racks, test-stand frames and the structures that support them. Those items cycle in load, and fatigue cracks start at their surfaces.

The public side of the region also generates MT work. Hospitals and universities run steel stacks, support structures and lifting equipment, and utility plants have pressure vessels and piping welds in carbon steel. The Connecticut Department of Transportation is rehabilitating the I-84 viaduct bridges in downtown Hartford to correct superstructure and substructure deterioration, and welded bridge details are classic MT territory because fatigue cracking begins at weld toes and connection plates. Rail corridors and river crossings add to the mix.

Typical MT targets here therefore include weld toes on frames and cranes, lifting lugs and hooks, rotating shaft shoulders, keyways and splines in carbon steel, nozzle welds on carbon-steel vessels, support brackets, and repair welds. Where a part is critical to a customer's product, MT is also used on tooling and fixtures as part of a plant's own maintenance program, under the customer's or plant's approved procedure.

What MT finds and what it cannot find

MT depends on magnetism. When ferromagnetic steel is magnetized, a crack at or just below the surface interrupts the flux and creates a leakage field that attracts fine iron particles. They collect over the crack and make a bright, readable line. The method is therefore limited to materials that can be magnetized: carbon steel and most low-alloy and martensitic steels. It will not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, titanium or nickel alloys, which dominate many aerospace parts, so those components need penetrant testing instead.

The method also has depth and direction limits. It is very sensitive to tight surface cracks and fades quickly with depth, so a deeply buried flaw may escape. Because a crack is found best when the field crosses it, each area is examined twice with the field turned about ninety degrees. Rough surfaces, heavy paint and magnetic writing from contact with other magnets create nonrelevant indications that the technician must sort out. If the question is internal flaws or wall loss, ultrasonic testing in Hartford is the better tool. A broader introduction is in our magnetic particle testing guide and on the national MT page.

Codes, customer requirements and Connecticut rules

The method follows the governing document. ASME Section V Article 7 provides the examination requirements for yokes, particles, field strength checks, lighting and coverage. Acceptance comes from the construction or service code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, and AWS D1.5 for state bridge steel. ASTM E709 is the guide to magnetic particle examination and ASTM E1444 is the practice. Our article on ASME Section V Article 7 summarizes the main points.

In Connecticut, boilers are inspected under Chapter 540 of the General Statutes, which provides for state inspectors, insurance company inspectors and special inspectors, and the Office of the State Building Inspector administers the program. How a given vessel falls under it should be confirmed with the jurisdiction and your insurer. MT after weld repair is a standard acceptance step, and Atlantis reports the indications while the authorized inspector and repair organization retain their own responsibilities.

Aerospace-related suppliers often receive procedures or specifications from their own customers. If a customer document governs the MT you need, send it with the quote request so we can confirm what the procedure and report must contain. We work to the approved procedure you provide or to one our ASNT Level III writes against the code, and we do not state that SNT-TC-1A qualification alone satisfies any particular customer.

Technique: yokes, particles and light

Field MT in Hartford typically uses an electromagnetic yoke. Under Article 7 an alternating-current yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and we verify that with a test weight. Prods are used only where a yoke cannot reach, since contact burns can damage finished surfaces. Wet particles in a carrier give the highest sensitivity on machined and critical surfaces, while dry powder is practical on rough welds and in outdoor settings.

Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, so we plan an enclosure, a shaded corner or a work bay before the job. Visible particles with a contrast paint are the alternative where darkness is not available. A field indicator confirms that the magnetic field is oriented correctly in the part, and the technician examines each area in two directions.

Demagnetization is required when residual magnetism could attract chips, disturb arc welding or affect bearings and instruments. The procedure states the requirement and how the field is checked afterward. Parts are wiped clear of particles when the examination is complete.

Fatigue cracking, lifting equipment and bridge details

Lifting equipment and welded structures deserve special attention because their failures are sudden. Hooks, shackles, spreader beams, crane girders, press frames and hoist supports carry thousands of load cycles, and the cracks that grow in them start at the surface, usually at a weld toe, a sharp corner or a hole edge. Highway bridge details behave the same way: attachment welds and connection plates concentrate stress and are classic places for fatigue cracks. MT is the practical field method to look at these locations because it is quick, sensitive to tight surface cracks and needs only access to the steel.

For crane and below-the-hook equipment, owners usually schedule periodic examinations as part of their inspection routines, with scope and acceptance set by the responsible engineer. For bridge work, scope and acceptance come from the owner's specification. We perform the examination to the procedure, record every indication, and leave the decision on repair or removal from service with the owner and engineer.

Verifying the process before and during the job

Before examining production items, the technician checks that the equipment and consumables work. The yoke is tested with a test weight, the particle suspension concentration is checked when wet particles are used, and a field indicator or reference piece confirms the field is strong enough and correctly oriented. Lighting at the surface is measured for visible work, and for fluorescent work the UV-A intensity and ambient white light are checked. These checks are written in the report, so a reviewer can see that the method was capable of finding what it was supposed to find.

Surface preparation, indications and acceptance

Oil, grease, scale and heavy paint reduce sensitivity and must be removed in the examination area. Rough weld caps may need light grinding. The technician classifies each indication as relevant or nonrelevant, measures the relevant ones and compares them with the acceptance criteria. Linear indications generally indicate cracks, while rounded indications often indicate porosity. Doubtful indications are removed and re-examined to see if they return.

Who performs the inspection

Atlantis has no office in Hartford. Technicians are mobilized from outside Connecticut and travel to your site for the scope we agree. They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, which places certification with the employer. Level II technicians perform and interpret the work, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and signs off the reports. If your contract specifies qualification evidence, tell us before the work starts.

What the report contains

The report records the component and the areas examined, the procedure number and revision, technique, yoke or current type, particles and carrier, lighting, equipment checks, the technician and level, date and surface condition. Each indication is listed with location, orientation and length, with accept or reject against the named criteria, and sketches or photographs mark where it sits. Areas examined with no indications are noted so coverage is proven.

Planning an MT job in Hartford

Winter in the Connecticut River valley is cold and damp. Steel temperature affects carrier fluids and visibility, and outdoor crane runways or bridge members may need a procedure for low temperatures or a warmer window. Summer heat can make exposed steel too hot for wet methods, where dry powder and shade help. Wet weather complicates yard and bridge work.

Access planning matters. Lift equipment, scaffolding, fall protection and traffic control for highway work are arranged with the owner or contractor. Hospitals, universities and manufacturing plants often need escorts, background checks and tool inventories before contractors enter. I-84 and I-91 meet in Hartford, and construction can affect travel; we agree timing with your supervisor rather than promising an arrival window.

MT, PT or UT: choosing the method in Hartford

Choose MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Hartford for stainless, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys. Choose UT for thickness and internal weld flaws. Our MT versus PT comparison explains how the two surface methods differ.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers in the capital region can qualify their own people. Our MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training are taught by an ASNT Level III. The training page for East Hartford explains delivery for Connecticut employers, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the hours and experience your written practice may require.

faq.q: Which materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: MT works only on ferromagnetic steels such as carbon and low-alloy steel. Stainless steel, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys cannot be magnetized, so those parts need liquid penetrant testing or another method instead.

faq.q: What defects does MT find on bridge steel and plant structures in Hartford?
faq.a: It finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, laps and lack of fusion, especially fatigue cracks at weld toes, connection plates, lifting lugs and shaft shoulders where cyclic loading starts cracking at the surface.

faq.q: Why is each area examined in two directions?
faq.a: A crack produces the strongest indication when the magnetic field crosses it at a right angle. Examining each area twice with the field turned about ninety degrees reveals cracks running in any direction.

faq.q: Do you use dry powder or wet fluorescent particles?
faq.a: Dry powder suits rough welds, outdoor work and warm steel, while wet fluorescent particles are more sensitive on machined and critical surfaces but need a darkened area under UV-A light. The choice follows your procedure and site conditions.

faq.q: When is demagnetization needed after MT?
faq.a: Demagnetization is needed when residual magnetism could attract chips, disturb welding or affect bearings and instruments. The procedure states the requirement, and we check the remaining field when it applies.

faq.q: Can MT be performed on tooling and fixtures at an aerospace supplier?
faq.a: Yes, if the part is ferromagnetic and the procedure allows it. We work to your approved procedure or one written against the code, and we need any customer document that governs the examination.

faq.q: How do I request MT inspection in the Hartford area?
faq.a: Send the part or weld type, material, governing code or customer document, quantity, access conditions and site rules through the quote form. Crews visit your premises for the scope we settle on together, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Who qualifies the technicians who perform MT?
faq.a: The company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, sets out who may do what. Level II staff carry out the testing, while procedures and report review sit with an ASNT Level III.

faq.q: Can you train our staff to perform MT?
faq.a: Yes. MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses are taught by an ASNT Level III, and our consulting team can help you draft the written practice your company uses to qualify and certify its own technicians.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Hartford, CT | Liquid PT
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing of stainless, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloy welds and parts in Hartford and Connecticut. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Hartford, Connecticut
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Hartford and the capital region for liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, on welds, castings, machined components and fabricated equipment. PT reveals cracks, laps, porosity and pinholes that are open to the surface of non-porous metals, which makes it the practical surface method for stainless steel, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys. Send the PT quote request for Hartford with the material, surface condition, procedure or customer specification, and quantity.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Hartford

Connecticut's aerospace cluster explains why PT matters here. Engine and aircraft systems work around East Hartford, Middletown and Windsor Locks depends on non-magnetic alloys: nickel superalloys, titanium, aluminum and stainless steel. Magnetic particle inspection cannot examine those materials, so penetrant processes are the standard surface method across the sector. Production examination of aerospace parts is normally carried out by the manufacturer under its customer's approved process. On-site PT from Atlantis fits other needs around those plants: fabricated equipment, tooling, utility piping, repair welds and maintenance checks performed under the plant's or the customer's approved procedure.

Elsewhere in the capital region, PT serves hospital and university energy plants, where stainless steel piping and heat exchangers sit in boiler rooms and utility tunnels, and mechanical contractors who weld stainless and aluminum. Machine shops check cutting-tool holders, fixtures and aluminum components. Bridge and structural work uses PT on non-ferrous or stainless details and as a second look at weld repairs where magnetic examination is awkward.

Older equipment also sits in many Connecticut plants. Aging aluminum castings, stainless tubes and brazed assemblies are often examined before a production restart or a modification, and a penetrant check of accessible surfaces gives an early read on cracking.

What PT finds and what it misses

PT relies on capillary action. A thin penetrant is applied to a clean surface and left to dwell, then removed from the surface so that only liquid trapped in discontinuities remains. A developer draws it out and spreads it into a visible indication. Only discontinuities that are open to the surface can be found, so subsurface cracks, buried lack of fusion and wall loss are outside the method. A crack smeared shut by grinding, shot peening or machining may hold no penetrant at all, which is why cleaning and etching practice matter for finished parts.

Porous surfaces trap penetrant everywhere and hide indications, and rough or oily surfaces cause heavy background. Over-removal can wash penetrant out of fine cracks, while under-removal leaves a background that obscures them. When the concern is internal, ultrasonic testing in Hartford is the right method, and for surface cracks in carbon steel magnetic particle inspection in Hartford is often faster. The national liquid penetrant testing page covers the method in general.

Codes, customer requirements and Connecticut rules

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the requirements for materials, process times, preparation, temperature and evaluation. Acceptance comes from the governing code: Mandatory Appendix 8 of ASME Section VIII Division 1 for vessels, paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 of ASME B31.3 for piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 for structural and stainless welds. ASTM E165 is the general industry practice that many owner specifications reference. See our explainer on ASME Section V Article 6 for a closer look.

Connecticut regulates boilers through Chapter 540 of its General Statutes, with state inspectors, insurance company inspectors and special inspectors, and the Office of the State Building Inspector administers the program. Confirm with the jurisdiction and your insurer how each vessel is classified. After repair welding, PT is a common acceptance check, and Atlantis records the indications for the responsible inspector.

Many suppliers work to flow-down requirements from their customers. If a customer specification, such as an approved penetrant process or material list, governs the work, send it with your request. We write or follow a procedure against it, and we do not say that SNT-TC-1A qualification by itself satisfies any particular customer. Aerospace production examination lines have their own process controls, and we do not replace them.

Technique: penetrant types, removal and development

Penetrants are classed by dye and removal. Type I is fluorescent, viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, and Type II is visible dye, viewed under white light. Fluorescent systems are more sensitive and suit critical parts; visible systems suit field work. Removal can be by water wash, post-emulsification or solvent wipe. Solvent-removable materials are the usual field choice, because they need no running water and allow careful removal with lint-free wipes.

The sequence is steady. Clean and dry the surface. Apply penetrant for the dwell time in the procedure. Remove the excess without disturbing the liquid in flaws. Apply developer, either dry powder, water-suspended or a non-aqueous suspension. Allow development, then examine. The technician distinguishes cracks and linear indications from rounded porosity and false indications from scratches, wiping streaks or incomplete cleaning. Test panels and system checks show the materials are working before the job.

Material control for nickel, titanium and stainless alloys

Special alloys call for care. Penetrant, developer and cleaner for nickel alloys, titanium and austenitic stainless steel are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, because residues can promote cracking at elevated temperature or in service. Procedures call for a thorough post-clean so that no penetrant or developer remains in cracks or crevices. Material certifications for consumables are kept with the job record and referenced in the report. If your specification names approved consumables, tell us before mobilization so that we bring the right materials.

Temperature and cleanliness in a New England climate

Article 6 treats roughly 5 to 52 degrees Celsius as the standard range for the part and the materials, and working outside that band requires a procedure qualified for the temperature in use. Connecticut winters can chill outdoor steel below the band and summer sun can push it above, so exterior piping, tanks and structural details need planning around the weather. Wind and dust carry debris onto cleaned surfaces, so a windbreak or a covered bay helps.

Welds, repairs and hold points

Most field PT is attached to welding. After a repair, a defect is ground out, the cavity is examined, the weld is made and the finished surface is examined again. On critical stainless or nickel-alloy piping a root pass may be examined before filler passes cover it, because a crack found then costs minutes to fix, whereas the same crack found after pressure testing costs days. Tell us about the hold points in your weld plan so the examination fits the welding sequence instead of delaying it.

Reading a penetrant indication correctly

Interpretation is the skill that separates a useful report from a confusing one. A crack bleeds out as a sharp, continuous line that grows as more liquid emerges. Porosity shows as scattered round dots, and lack of fusion at the edge of a weld appears as an intermittent line. Scratches, tool marks and wiping streaks can look similar, so the technician wipes a doubtful indication and re-applies developer to see whether it returns in the same place and shape. We list the indications we dismissed, with the reason, so a reviewer can follow the reasoning.

Tooling, fixtures and maintenance checks

Not every examination is on a finished product. Machine shops and test facilities in the Hartford area use fixtures, holders, adapters and rigging in aluminum, stainless and other non-magnetic metals, and these items crack in service from repeated clamping and vibration. A planned penetrant check of high-stress areas, performed under the plant's own procedure, finds cracks before a fixture damages a part or injures an operator. We can set up a recurring survey that covers the same areas each time, with a record that shows condition over time.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Hartford. Crews head out to your plant for the work we define together. They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which the employer certifies. Level II technicians prepare and verify the process, run the examination and interpret indications, while an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the component and area examined, the procedure number and revision, penetrant, remover and developer by type and batch, dwell and development times, surface temperature, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is described by location, type, size and orientation and judged against the named criteria. Photographs or sketches show where it sits, and a note records post-cleaning. Areas with no indications are listed so coverage is clear.

Documentation that holds up to a customer audit

Suppliers in the aerospace chain are audited by their customers, and an examination record is only as persuasive as its traceability. Our PT record ties each indication or clear area to a part or weld identifier, the procedure revision, the consumable batch numbers and the technician's qualification level. When your auditor asks how a result was produced, the answer is in the file, not in anyone's memory. If your quality manual specifies a report format or record retention rule, tell us at quote stage and we will fit the report to it.

Planning a PT job in Hartford

Cold slows penetrant and thickens solvents, heat flashes liquids off too soon, and fluorescent work needs a dim area, so tents or dim rooms are arranged in advance. faq.q: Do dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing mean the same thing?
faq.a: They do. PT is the formal name used in codes and procedures, while shop floors say dye penetrant for the same visible or fluorescent dye process that makes surface-breaking flaws show up.

faq.q: Why is PT used so often on aerospace-related alloys?
faq.a: Nickel alloys, titanium, aluminum and stainless steel cannot be magnetized, so magnetic particle inspection does not work on them. Penetrant methods detect surface-breaking flaws on those non-porous materials.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find flaws below the surface?
faq.a: No. PT only finds discontinuities open to the surface. Buried cracks, internal lack of fusion and wall loss need ultrasonic testing, and surface smearing from grinding or machining can hide shallow cracks.

faq.q: Do you control consumables for nickel and titanium work?
faq.a: Yes, when the specification requires it we use penetrant, developer and cleaner controlled for halogen and sulfur content, keep material certifications with the job record and post-clean thoroughly to remove residues.

faq.q: How does Connecticut weather affect PT?
faq.a: Penetrant behaves best within a defined temperature band. Colder or hotter outdoor steel needs a procedure qualified for that temperature or a different schedule, and wind or dust calls for a windbreak or covered work area.

faq.q: Can you perform PT under a customer-approved process?
faq.a: We can follow an approved procedure you supply or write one against the code, but we need the customer document up front. Production process lines at manufacturers have their own controls, and we do not replace them.
